question.text: what if a program were a list of orders that keep changing what is in memory?

metaphor.text: a cooking recipe, with steps in order that transform the ingredients. It stops working at one point: a recipe asks nothing, and a program can.

history.text: in 1945, John von Neumann described a computer that keeps the program in its memory, together with the data. In 1957, John Backus's team published FORTRAN, one of the first languages that let you write those orders as formulas.

cost.text: to know what a box holds you have to follow the orders in sequence, one by one.

runs.text: The age goes in; the price comes out. The possible ages split into two regions: those who pay 5 and those who pay 8. Between them there is an edge, between 11 and 12.

blocks.description: A line of ages from 0 to 100 split into two regions: those who pay 5, up to 11, and those who pay 8, from 12. A red line marks the edge between 11 and 12, with a point on each side.

caption.text: Two regions and an edge. Each region needs a case; the edge, one on each side.

points.text: A paradigm is a way of organising a program; in imperative programming, the program is a list of orders that change memory.
A condition is a question whose answer is a boolean value:
A decision runs only one of the paths; the current instruction skips the other.
A case partition splits the inputs into regions; you test one case per region and both sides of each edge.
